surface_mechanism_description: The growth of ZnO films is accomplished by trapping a volume of dimethylzinc (DMZ) and nitrogen mixture between the 2-position and 12-position valves, allowing it to expand into the reaction chamber and react with the heated substrate. A subsequent nitrogen gas flush oxidizes the DMZ on the surface of the substrate. Another volume of dimethylzinc vapor is trapped and the process repeats. The growth of zinc sulfide is more complicated, requiring hydrogen sulfide to convert the zinc oxide film to zinc sulfide. The system operation involves careful control of the nitrogen flush pressure and hydrogen sulfide pressure to ensure the correct stoichiometry of the films.
evidence: The growth of ZnO films is easily accomplished in this system. First, a small volume of dimethylzinc (DMZ) and nitrogen mixture is trapped between the 2-position and 12-position valves. This volume is then allowed to expand into the reaction chamber and adsorb or react on the substrate. A subsequent flush with nitrogen gas oxidizes the DMZ (due to the trace impurities) on the surface of the substrate. Another volume of dimethylzinc vapor is trapped and the process repeats. The growth of zinc sulfide is slightly more complicated. The zinc oxide film first formed must be converted to zinc sulfide by hydrogen sulfide. This reaction does proceed readily. In practice, zinc sulfide is not obtained with a 30 psig hydrogen sulfide pressure. Pressures of up to 70 psig are required to obtain zinc sulfide films of reasonable stoichiometry.
